objectives.title: Understand the Automation Skill Authority (ASA) automation sprint cycle

Easy.scenario: You have been assigned your first module in the LMS. You read the theory, but you cannot proceed to the next module because the 'Module Gate Locked' screen appears.
Easy.q: What is the primary action required to unlock the next module in this specific LMS?
options: Wait for 24 hours.
Achieve an 80% or higher score on the current module's assessment quiz.
Ask an administrator for an access token.
Scroll to the bottom of all the lesson pages.
Easy.a: Achieve an 80% or higher score on the current module's assessment quiz.
Easy.explanation: This platform utilizes a Mastery-based learning system. You cannot progress to advanced modules until you prove technical competency (an 80% score) on the foundational prerequisites.

Easy.q: In the context of the Automation Skill Authority LMS, what is the purpose of the 'Telemetry' tracker?
options: To record your test execution speed in Playwright.
To log your learning progress, time spent, and unlocked achievements in the background.
To track mouse movements for anti-cheat purposes.
To monitor the uptime of the LMS servers.
Easy.a: To log your learning progress, time spent, and unlocked achievements in the background.
Easy.explanation: The telemetry system runs in the background of the application, logging significant learning events (like completing a module, breaking a streak, or earning a badge) to build your overall profile stats.

Easy.scenario: You are navigating the main dashboard and notice a section detailing your 'Streak'.
Easy.q: How does the streak mechanic influence your learning process? (Select all that apply)
options: It forces you to code every single day or you lose access to the platform.
It tracks consecutive days of logging into the platform to encourage consistent learning habits.
It rewards consistent engagement by tracking your 'Best Streak' over time.
It increases the difficulty of the quizzes automatically.
a: It tracks consecutive days of logging into the platform to encourage consistent learning habits.
It rewards consistent engagement by tracking your 'Best Streak' over time.
Easy.explanation: Streaks are purely a gamification mechanic designed to encourage daily engagement and habit-building. They do not penalize you with locked content or modify the technical difficulty of the assessments.

Easy.scenario: You complete an assessment, but you only score 60%. The system shows you the correct answers and explanations.
Easy.q: What happens when you refresh the page to retake the assessment?
options: You will receive the exact same 5 questions in the exact same order.
You will receive a newly randomized set of 5 questions pulled from the module's larger quiz pool.
You are locked out for 24 hours.
The system will only ask you the questions you got wrong.
Easy.a: You will receive a newly randomized set of 5 questions pulled from the module's larger quiz pool.
Easy.explanation: To prevent simple memorization of answers (A, C, B, D), the assessment engine dynamically shuffles and selects a new combination of Easy, Medium, and Hard questions from a larger pool on every attempt.

Easy.q: Where does the LMS permanently store this progress data by default for a local user?
options: In a remote AWS server.
In a local SQLite database accessed via the `/api/progress` endpoint.
In the browser's cookies.
In a text file on the desktop.
Easy.a: In a local SQLite database accessed via the `/api/progress` endpoint.
Easy.explanation: The platform utilizes a backend database (like Prisma/SQLite) to permanently store user progress. This ensures that if you clear your browser cache, your mastery and unlocked modules remain intact.

Medium.scenario: You are viewing the dashboard on your laptop, but you decide to switch to your mobile phone to read a lesson. When you log in on your phone, your progress is missing.
Medium.q: How can you synchronize your progress between your laptop and your mobile device?
options: Connect them via a USB cable.
Use the 'Mobile Sync' QR code feature on the dashboard to transfer your encrypted profile payload.
You cannot sync progress; you must start over.
Email the database file to yourself.
Medium.a: Use the 'Mobile Sync' QR code feature on the dashboard to transfer your encrypted profile payload.
Medium.explanation: The LMS includes a 'Sync Profile' feature. By scanning the QR code generated on your primary device, you can securely transfer your `userId` and progress data payload to the new device via the `/api/progress/sync` endpoint.

Medium.scenario: You are exploring the 'Professional Track' feature on the dashboard.
Medium.q: What is the primary architectural purpose of mapping modules to Professional Tracks? (Select all that apply)
options: To provide a curated, role-specific learning path (e.g., SDET vs QA Analyst).
To prevent users from taking modules outside their assigned track.
To align technical assessments with real-world enterprise job requirements.
To charge different prices for different tracks.
a: To provide a curated, role-specific learning path (e.g., SDET vs QA Analyst).
To align technical assessments with real-world enterprise job requirements.
Medium.explanation: Tracks exist to guide learners through the specific set of skills required for targeted industry roles. They organize content logically without strictly restricting access to cross-disciplinary learning.

Medium.q: Based on this core LMS logic, what happens if a user completes Module 1 and Module 3, but skips Module 2?
options: Module 3 will become locked the next time they refresh the page.
Module 4 will remain locked until Module 2 is completed.
The system will crash.
The user will be awarded the completion badge for Module 3.
Medium.a: Module 4 will remain locked until Module 2 is completed.
Medium.explanation: The logic iterates through *all* preceding modules. Even if a user somehow bypassed the UI to complete Module 3, Module 4 checks indices 0, 1, 2, and 3. Since Module 2 is incomplete, Module 4 evaluates to locked.

Medium.scenario: A new user tries to submit an assessment. They select all the right answers, but the network connection drops exactly when they click 'Submit'.
Medium.q: What is the expected behavior of the LMS state management in this scenario?
options: The UI will show the module as completed, but upon refresh, it will revert to locked because the database was not updated.
The browser will automatically retry the submission for 24 hours.
The LMS will crash and delete their account.
The local state will save it permanently without the database.
Medium.a: The UI will show the module as completed, but upon refresh, it will revert to locked because the database was not updated.
Medium.explanation: If the API call to `/api/progress` fails due to network loss, the backend database never records the score. Because the LMS relies on the backend as the single source of truth upon reload, the progress will be lost.

Medium.scenario: You are reading a highly technical module on Playwright Architecture. The module contains code snippets, diagrams, and theoretical explanations.
Medium.q: Which of the following elements does the LMS use to present this content dynamically? (Select all that apply)
options: Markdown (MDX) for rich text and embedded components.
Syntax-highlighted code blocks.
Interactive quizzes injected directly at the bottom of the page.
A live, embedded Virtual Machine running Linux.
Flash animations.
a: Markdown (MDX) for rich text and embedded components.
Syntax-highlighted code blocks.
Interactive quizzes injected directly at the bottom of the page.
Medium.explanation: The platform is built using MDX (Markdown + JSX), allowing it to seamlessly blend standard markdown (text, code blocks) with interactive React components (like the Assessment Engine) directly inside the lesson flow. It does not use VMs or Flash.

Hard.q: An administrator changes the backend to require a 100% score for certification. They update the API, but users are still unlocking modules with an 80% score. Based on the code above, why is this happening?
options: The frontend Zustand store (`useMasteryStore`) has hardcoded the pass threshold logic (`p.score >= 80`) locally instead of relying on a backend status flag.
The API is caching the old responses.
The `completedModules` array is read-only.
The browser's local storage is overriding the fetch call.
Hard.a: The frontend Zustand store (`useMasteryStore`) has hardcoded the pass threshold logic (`p.score >= 80`) locally instead of relying on a backend status flag.
Hard.explanation: This is a classic architectural decoupling flaw. The frontend is interpreting the raw score and making the business decision (`>= 80`) itself. To fix this, the backend API should evaluate the score and simply return a boolean `is_passed: true`, so the frontend doesn't hardcode business rules.

Hard.scenario: You want to design a custom curriculum path that bypasses the linear module locking system for senior engineers taking a fast-track assessment.
Hard.q: Which architectural modifications would be necessary to support this without breaking the existing linear experience for junior engineers? (Select all that apply)
options: Add a `prerequisites` array property to each object in `modules.json` instead of relying on array index order.
Update the `isModuleLocked` function to check specific prerequisites instead of iterating through all previous indices.
Delete the `completedModules` array entirely.
Store the user's assigned 'track' (e.g., 'Senior') in the database and conditionally bypass locks.
Change all modules to level 1.
a: Add a `prerequisites` array property to each object in `modules.json` instead of relying on array index order.
Update the `isModuleLocked` function to check specific prerequisites instead of iterating through all previous indices.
Store the user's assigned 'track' (e.g., 'Senior') in the database and conditionally bypass locks.
Hard.explanation: Currently, the locking mechanism assumes a strict linear path (Index 0 must be done before Index 1). To support complex, non-linear tracks, you must decouple order from locking by using explicit `prerequisites: ['module-a']` and conditionally evaluating locks based on user roles.

Hard.scenario: A user complains that every time they complete a module, the entire website flashes white and reloads for a split second, causing a jarring user experience.
Hard.q: As the frontend architect, you trace this bug to a background synchronization call. What React/Zustand pattern was implemented incorrectly?
options: Setting `loading: true` globally during a background data fetch, which triggered a top-level unmount/remount of the layout components.
Using `fetch()` instead of `axios()`.
Failing to use `React.memo` on the Quiz component.
Storing progress in local storage synchronously.
Hard.a: Setting `loading: true` globally during a background data fetch, which triggered a top-level unmount/remount of the layout components.
Hard.explanation: If a global `loading` state is tied to the main `<Layout>` component, toggling it to `true` during a silent background sync will cause the layout to render a spinner, effectively unmounting and remounting the entire DOM tree.

Hard.q: Why does this specific sequence of operations theoretically allow a user to see the explanations for the questions *before* the backend has actually confirmed their score was saved?
options: `completeModule` is an asynchronous function (returns a Promise), but it is not being `await`ed. Therefore, `setIsSubmitted(true)` fires synchronously and instantly updates the UI.
The backend is faster than the React state update.
`setIsSubmitted` is an asynchronous React hook.
It is impossible for the UI to update before the backend responds.
Hard.a: `completeModule` is an asynchronous function (returns a Promise), but it is not being `await`ed. Therefore, `setIsSubmitted(true)` fires synchronously and instantly updates the UI.
Hard.explanation: Because `completeModule` is fired and not awaited, the execution context immediately moves to the next line, setting `isSubmitted` to true. This triggers a React re-render, showing the explanations instantly, regardless of whether the network request to the database succeeds, fails, or hangs.

Hard.scenario: You want to add an 'Achievements' system that awards a 'Night Owl' badge if a user completes a module between 1:00 AM and 4:00 AM local time.
Hard.q: To ensure this feature cannot be easily cheated by a user simply changing their computer's clock, where must the time validation logic execute?
options: Inside the `/api/progress` backend route, utilizing the server's clock and comparing it against the user's timezone offset payload.
Inside the `useMasteryStore` Zustand state manager.
Inside the React component `useEffect` hook.
By querying an external NTP server from the browser before submitting.
Hard.a: Inside the `/api/progress` backend route, utilizing the server's clock and comparing it against the user's timezone offset payload.
Hard.explanation: Client-side clocks (JS `new Date()`) are trivial to manipulate. Security and validation logic—such as awarding time-based or secure badges—must always be executed on a trusted backend environment (Node.js API) that relies on a secure server clock.

meta.outcome: Master the Automation Skill Authority (ASA) CLI and environment variables

Easy.scenario: You are writing a new test locally and want to see the browser interactions, but your playwright.config.ts is set to headless: true by default for CI.
Easy.q: Which CLI command allows you to view the browser without modifying the configuration file?
options: npx playwright test --ui
npx playwright test --headed
npx playwright test --show-browser
npx playwright test --debug
Easy.a: npx playwright test --headed
Easy.explanation: The `--headed` flag overrides the config file to force the browser to run visibly. While `--ui` and `--debug` also show the browser, they open additional inspection tools, which might not be what you want if you just want to watch the execution run.

Easy.q: A Junior SDET runs tests using `npx playwright test`. The tests immediately fail because the application navigates to 'about:blank'. What is missing?
options: The STAGING_URL environment variable was not set in the shell or .env file before running the tests.
baseURL cannot be configured inside the 'use' block.
process.env is not accessible in TypeScript config files.
The defineConfig block is missing the 'projects' array.
Easy.a: The STAGING_URL environment variable was not set in the shell or .env file before running the tests.
Easy.explanation: If `process.env.STAGING_URL` is undefined (because the `.env` file wasn't loaded or the variable wasn't exported in the shell), Playwright's `baseURL` becomes undefined, causing `page.goto('/')` to fail or resolve to `about:blank`.

Easy.scenario: Your suite has 50 tests. You want to run only the tests tagged with '@smoke' on the 'Mobile Safari' project.
Easy.q: Which CLI flags must you combine to achieve this? (Select all that apply)
options: --grep @smoke
--project="Mobile Safari"
--tag @smoke
--device="iPhone 13"
--filter @smoke
a: --grep @smoke
--project="Mobile Safari"
Easy.explanation: Playwright uses `--grep` (or `-g`) to run tests matching a specific title or tag pattern. The `--project` flag targets a specific project defined in your `playwright.config.ts`. The other flags do not exist in the standard CLI.

Easy.scenario: You pushed your code, and the GitHub Action pipeline is running. You want to ensure the pipeline stops immediately if 3 tests fail, rather than wasting 20 minutes running the rest.
Easy.q: Which configuration setting or CLI flag enforces this?
options: --max-failures=3
retries: 3
--stop-on-failure=3
fullyParallel: false
Easy.a: --max-failures=3
Easy.explanation: The `--max-failures=3` flag (or `maxFailures: 3` in the config) tells the Playwright test runner to abort the entire test suite as soon as the failure threshold is reached, saving valuable CI/CD compute minutes.

Easy.q: When diagnosing a flaky test suite that only fails in CI, why might an SDET temporarily run this command locally?
options: To force tests to run sequentially to rule out parallel data collisions.
To ensure the tests run on only 1 browser type.
To prevent the Playwright Inspector from opening multiple windows.
To reduce CPU usage on their local machine.
Easy.a: To force tests to run sequentially to rule out parallel data collisions.
Easy.explanation: Setting `--workers=1` disables parallel execution. If the tests pass consistently with 1 worker but fail with 4, it strongly indicates a race condition or shared state/data collision between tests.

Medium.q: A developer commits this config. The tests pass locally, but fail instantly in the GitHub Actions pipeline. Why?
options: .env.local is typically ignored by git, meaning the CI server cannot find it to load the variables.
dotenv does not work in CI/CD pipelines.
process.env cannot be overridden by dotenv.
The path must be absolute (e.g., path.resolve('.env.local')).
Medium.a: .env.local is typically ignored by git, meaning the CI server cannot find it to load the variables.
Medium.explanation: Files like `.env.local` contain local developer secrets and are universally added to `.gitignore`. Because it is not committed to the repository, `dotenv` fails silently in CI, resulting in an undefined `BASE_URL`. CI environments should rely on injected environment variables/secrets instead of `.env` files.

Medium.scenario: Your CI pipeline is taking 45 minutes to run. You have 3 GitHub Action runners available. You want to shard the test suite across all 3 runners.
Medium.q: Which of the following CLI commands are required on the CI runners to achieve this? (Select all that apply)
options: npx playwright test --shard=1/3
npx playwright test --shard=2/3
npx playwright test --shard=3/3
npx playwright test --parallel=3
npx playwright test --split=3
a: npx playwright test --shard=1/3
npx playwright test --shard=2/3
npx playwright test --shard=3/3
Medium.explanation: Playwright's native sharding requires passing the shard fraction to each respective CI node. Node 1 gets `--shard=1/3`, Node 2 gets `--shard=2/3`, etc. The flags `--parallel` and `--split` do not exist for sharding.

Medium.scenario: You are running tests against a staging environment that is notoriously slow today. Your locators are timing out after 30 seconds. You want to temporarily increase the timeout to 60 seconds without committing changes to the `playwright.config.ts`.
Medium.q: What is the correct way to override the test timeout from the CLI?
options: npx playwright test --timeout=60000
TIMEOUT=60000 npx playwright test
npx playwright test --global-timeout=60000
npx playwright test --wait=60000
Medium.a: npx playwright test --timeout=60000
Medium.explanation: The `--timeout` CLI flag overrides the `timeout` value set in the config file. It expects the value in milliseconds. `--global-timeout` limits the total execution time of the entire suite, not individual tests.

Medium.q: What architectural intent does this configuration demonstrate?
options: It optimizes for fast local development while maximizing stability and preventing parallel collisions in CI.
It forces local tests to run sequentially and CI tests to run in parallel.
It disables retries entirely when running on GitHub Actions.
It causes the tests to run indefinitely in CI if a failure occurs.
Medium.a: It optimizes for fast local development while maximizing stability and preventing parallel collisions in CI.
Medium.explanation: Locally, `process.env.CI` is false, so `retries` is 0 (fast feedback) and `workers` is undefined (uses 50% of local CPU cores for fast parallel runs). In CI, `retries` is 2 (handles flakiness) and `workers` is 1 (sequential execution to avoid resource/data collisions on underpowered CI nodes).

Medium.scenario: A test fails in the CI pipeline. You download the HTML report, but there is no trace file available to debug the failure. Your config has `trace: 'on-first-retry'`.
Medium.q: Why is the trace file missing for this failed test?
options: The test failed on its very first attempt, and retries were set to 0, so a retry never happened.
Traces cannot be generated in headless mode.
The HTML report does not support embedding trace files.
The trace file exceeded the maximum file size limit.
Medium.a: The test failed on its very first attempt, and retries were set to 0, so a retry never happened.
Medium.explanation: The `on-first-retry` setting records a trace *only* when the test fails and runs a second time (the first retry). If `retries: 0` is set in the config, a retry never triggers, so the trace is never recorded. Use `retain-on-failure` if retries are 0.

Hard.q: A test suite utilizes this config to inject an authenticated `storageState`. The `global-setup.ts` file performs an API login and writes the cookies to `state.json`. However, when you run `npx playwright test`, the first test always fails due to an outdated session, but the subsequent tests pass. What is the architectural flaw?
options: Playwright loads the 'use' config before globalSetup finishes, so the first test uses an old state.json from a previous run.
globalSetup cannot write files to the disk.
storageState cannot be defined in the 'use' block.
The API login must be performed inside a beforeEach hook, not globalSetup.
Hard.a: Playwright loads the 'use' config before globalSetup finishes, so the first test uses an old state.json from a previous run.
Hard.explanation: This is a notorious race condition. If `state.json` exists from a previous run, Playwright's worker threads may read the file into memory *before* the `globalSetup` finishes overwriting it. To fix this, use project dependencies (`dependencies: ['setup']`) instead of `globalSetup`.

Hard.scenario: You are managing a mono-repo. Your Playwright config is located at `packages/e2e/playwright.config.ts`, but you are currently running commands from the root directory `/`.
Hard.q: Which of the following commands will successfully execute the tests using that specific config? (Select all that apply)
options: npx playwright test --config=packages/e2e/playwright.config.ts
cd packages/e2e && npx playwright test
npx playwright test --project=packages/e2e
npx playwright test packages/e2e/
npm run test --prefix packages/e2e
a: npx playwright test --config=packages/e2e/playwright.config.ts
cd packages/e2e && npx playwright test
Hard.explanation: You must either navigate to the directory where the config lives, or explicitly tell Playwright where the config is using the `--config` flag. Passing the folder path (`packages/e2e/`) tells it where the tests are, but it will still look for the config in the root unless specified.

Hard.scenario: Your enterprise requires testing against three environments: QA, Staging, and Production. You want developers to easily run `ENV=qa npx playwright test` without modifying the config file.
Hard.q: How should you design the `playwright.config.ts` to dynamically resolve the `baseURL` based on the `ENV` variable?
options: Create a dictionary mapping `{ qa: 'url1', staging: 'url2' }` and assign `baseURL: urls[process.env.ENV || 'qa']`.
Create three separate playwright.config files and use bash scripts to swap them out.
Use the CLI flag `--base-url=$ENV`.
Export a default async function that reads the database to get the URL.
Hard.a: Create a dictionary mapping `{ qa: 'url1', staging: 'url2' }` and assign `baseURL: urls[process.env.ENV || 'qa']`.
Hard.explanation: Dynamically resolving environment variables using a dictionary map inside `playwright.config.ts` is the standard enterprise pattern. It keeps configuration centralized, type-safe, and avoids the maintenance nightmare of managing multiple config files.

Hard.q: What is the primary architectural advantage of this 'Project Dependencies' pattern over using a `globalSetup` script?
options: It allows the setup script to utilize the full Playwright Test runner (fixtures, reporting, tracing) instead of a raw Node.js script.
It allows the setup script to run on a different CI server.
It prevents Playwright from running the setup script more than once globally.
It converts the setup script into a GitHub Action automatically.
Hard.a: It allows the setup script to utilize the full Playwright Test runner (fixtures, reporting, tracing) instead of a raw Node.js script.
Hard.explanation: `globalSetup` runs outside the Playwright Test runner, meaning you lose built-in fixtures (like `page`, `request`), traces, video recording, and HTML reporting. Using project dependencies runs your setup as a native test, giving you full debugging and reporting capabilities if the setup fails.

Hard.scenario: You configure Playwright to generate an HTML report, but you notice that the report is silently overwritten every time you run a different shard on your CI nodes. You need to combine the reports at the end of the pipeline.
Hard.q: Which configuration/flag pattern is REQUIRED to successfully merge sharded Playwright reports in a CI environment?
options: Set the reporter to `['blob']` on the CI shards, then run `npx playwright merge-reports` in a final job.
Set the reporter to `['html']` and use `--merge` on the shards.
Configure the HTML reporter to append using `{ append: true }`.
Zip the `playwright-report` folders from all shards and extract them into the same directory.
Hard.a: Set the reporter to `['blob']` on the CI shards, then run `npx playwright merge-reports` in a final job.
Hard.explanation: HTML reports cannot be cleanly appended or zipped together because of embedded assets and state. Playwright introduced the `blob` reporter specifically for sharding. Shards output `.zip` blob files, which a final CI job collects and merges into a unified HTML report using `npx playwright merge-reports`.

Easy.scenario: You clone a Playwright repository and immediately run `npx playwright test`. The runner immediately fails, stating that it cannot find the 'playwright' module.
Easy.q: What fundamental setup step was skipped?
options: You must run `npm install` to download the dependencies listed in `package.json` into the `node_modules` directory.
You must run `npx playwright install` to download the browsers.
You need to globally install Playwright using `npm install -g playwright`.
You forgot to set the `NODE_ENV` environment variable.
Easy.a: You must run `npm install` to download the dependencies listed in `package.json` into the `node_modules` directory.
Easy.explanation: Cloning a repository only downloads the source code. You must explicitly run `npm install` (or `npm ci`) to download the external libraries (including Playwright itself) into your local `node_modules` folder before running any commands.

Easy.code:
git clone https://github.com/asa/framework.git
cd framework
npm install
npx playwright test
Easy.q: The developer followed these steps, but Playwright threw a fatal error: `browserType.launch: Executable doesn't exist at /Library/Caches/ms-playwright/chromium-1064/chrome-mac/Chromium.app`.
options: The developer forgot to run `npx playwright install` to download the actual browser binaries.
The developer is on an unsupported operating system.
The developer must run `npm run build` before testing.
The developer forgot to pass the `--headed` flag.
Easy.a: The developer forgot to run `npx playwright install` to download the actual browser binaries.
Easy.explanation: While `npm install` installs the Playwright test runner (the Node.js library), it does NOT automatically download the multi-gigabyte Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit browser binaries. You must explicitly run `npx playwright install` to fetch them into your system cache.

Easy.scenario: You are a lead engineer verifying that a junior tester's local environment is pointing to the correct enterprise GitHub repository before they push code.
Easy.q: Which of the following commands will successfully output the URL of the remote Git repository? (Select all that apply)
options: git remote -v
git config --get remote.origin.url
cat .git/config
git status
git branch -a
a: git remote -v
git config --get remote.origin.url
cat .git/config
Easy.explanation: The commands `git remote -v`, querying the git config directly, or manually reading the `.git/config` file will all reveal the upstream URL. `git status` shows working tree state, and `git branch -a` shows branches, not URLs.

Easy.scenario: You want to verify that the Node.js version installed on your machine matches the required version specified by your team (e.g., v20.x).
Easy.q: Which CLI command verifies your active Node.js version?
options: node -v
npm -v
npx node version
node --version-check
Easy.a: node -v
Easy.explanation: The `node -v` (or `node --version`) command outputs the currently active version of the Node.js runtime. `npm -v` outputs the version of the Node Package Manager, which is versioned separately from Node itself.

Easy.q: Given this `package.json` block, how do you execute the UI mode using NPM?
options: npm run test:ui
npx test:ui
npm start test:ui
node test:ui
Easy.a: npm run test:ui
Easy.explanation: Scripts defined in the `package.json` `scripts` block are executed using the `npm run <script-name>` command. Using `npx` attempts to download and run an external package, which will fail here.

Medium.scenario: You are debugging a flaky CI/CD pipeline. The pipeline runs `npm install` before executing tests. Sometimes tests fail mysteriously due to slightly different dependency versions being resolved.
Medium.q: What is the industry-standard architectural change to ensure dependencies are exactly identical to the developer's local machine?
options: Change `npm install` to `npm ci` in the CI pipeline.
Commit the `node_modules` folder to Git.
Use `npm install --exact` in the CI pipeline.
Use `npx npm-check-updates -u` before installing.
Medium.a: Change `npm install` to `npm ci` in the CI pipeline.
Medium.explanation: `npm ci` (clean install) ignores the `package.json` loose versioning and strictly installs the exact versions locked in `package-lock.json`. It also deletes the `node_modules` folder beforehand, ensuring a pristine, repeatable environment.

Medium.q: Why is the `cross-env` utility required in this npm script for enterprise compatibility?
options: It ensures the environment variable is set successfully regardless of whether the developer is using Windows, macOS, or Linux.
It allows Playwright to cross-test on Chromium, WebKit, and Firefox simultaneously.
It forces Playwright to bypass Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) security policies.
It compiles cross-platform TypeScript into JavaScript before running.
Medium.a: It ensures the environment variable is set successfully regardless of whether the developer is using Windows, macOS, or Linux.
Medium.explanation: Setting environment variables inline (e.g., `VAR=value command`) is native to Unix/Linux shells (bash/zsh) but fails natively in Windows Command Prompt. `cross-env` abstracts this difference, providing a unified syntax for all team members.

Medium.scenario: A developer reports that their local environment is completely broken after pulling a massive architecture refactor from the `main` branch. Files have been renamed, dependencies removed, and tests are failing.
Medium.q: Which of the following commands represent a safe, standard procedure to completely 'nuke and pave' the local environment to a pristine state? (Select all that apply)
options: rm -rf node_modules && rm package-lock.json
npm cache clean --force
npm install
git clean -fdx
git reset --hard HEAD
a: rm -rf node_modules && rm package-lock.json
npm cache clean --force
npm install
Medium.explanation: A standard 'nuke and pave' for Node environments involves deleting `node_modules` and the lockfile, forcing a cache clean, and reinstalling. While `git clean -fdx` is a powerful Git command to wipe untracked files, it aggressively deletes `.env` files and other local setups, requiring manual reconfiguration.

Medium.scenario: You are running tests in an isolated Docker container. The tests run, but any tests utilizing `page.screenshot()` fail because the fonts look like completely broken square blocks (often called 'tofu').
Medium.q: What environmental dependency is missing from the container?
options: The container OS is missing system-level fonts.
The container needs the `--headed` flag to render screenshots.
Playwright requires a dedicated GPU to render screenshots.
The Chromium binary was not downloaded correctly.
Medium.a: The container OS is missing system-level fonts.
Medium.explanation: Minimal Linux Docker images (like Ubuntu Core or Alpine) do not come with standard fonts installed. Hard.q: You are building a Docker image to run your tests in AWS Fargate. You notice that the build process is extremely slow because it reinstalls all NPM packages every time you change a single line of test code. Why is this happening?
options: Because `COPY . .` copies the entire directory, invalidating the Docker cache for the `RUN npm ci` layer whenever any file changes.
Because `npm ci` is inherently slower than `npm install` inside Docker containers.
Because you did not run `npx playwright install` inside the Dockerfile.
Because the Microsoft Playwright base image is too large.
Hard.a: Because `COPY . .` copies the entire directory, invalidating the Docker cache for the `RUN npm ci` layer whenever any file changes.
Hard.explanation: Docker builds layers sequentially and caches them. By placing `COPY package*.json ./` followed by `RUN npm ci` *before* copying the rest of the source code (`COPY . .`), Docker caches the node_modules layer. It will only rerun `npm ci` if the `package.json` actually changes, not when test files change.

Hard.scenario: You are migrating a legacy Selenium project to Playwright. The project has hundreds of obsolete NPM packages. You want to execute Playwright, but you want to absolutely guarantee that your new Playwright tests are not secretly relying on any globally installed Node modules on your machine.

Uninstall Node.js and reinstall it.
Run `npm uninstall -g` for every package.
Use a virtual machine.
Hard.a: Run the tests using `npx` inside a newly cloned folder with no global modules installed, relying strictly on the local `node_modules`.
Hard.explanation: The core design philosophy of `npx` is that it executes binaries strictly from the local `node_modules/.bin` directory. By combining a fresh clone, a pristine `npm ci`, and `npx playwright test`, you categorically eliminate global state pollution.

meta.outcome: Handle common Git and dependency conflicts

Easy.scenario: You run `npm install` and receive a massive wall of red text complaining about 'ERESOLVE unable to resolve dependency tree' and 'peer dependencies'.
Easy.q: What is the industry-standard initial command to bypass strict peer dependency conflicts in legacy projects?
options: npm install --legacy-peer-deps
npm install --force
npm audit fix --force
rm package-lock.json && npm install
Easy.a: npm install --legacy-peer-deps
Easy.explanation: NPM v7+ introduced strict peer dependency resolution, which often breaks legacy projects. Using `--legacy-peer-deps` tells NPM to ignore peer dependency conflicts and install anyway. Using `--force` is dangerous as it fetches different versions and breaks the lockfile.

Easy.code:
git checkout feature-login
git rebase main
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in tests/login.spec.ts
Easy.q: You are rebasing your branch onto main, but encounter a merge conflict. After opening the file, resolving the `<<<<<<<` and `>>>>>>>` markers, what are the exact next two commands you must run?
options: git add tests/login.spec.ts  followed by  git rebase --continue
git commit -m 'resolved'  followed by  git push
git rebase --skip  followed by  git merge
git add tests/login.spec.ts  followed by  git commit
Easy.a: git add tests/login.spec.ts  followed by  git rebase --continue
Easy.explanation: During a rebase, you never create a 'merge commit' to resolve conflicts. You simply stage the resolved file using `git add`, and then tell git to proceed with the rebase using `git rebase --continue`.

Easy.scenario: A colleague is confused about the difference between merging and rebasing when updating their feature branch with the latest changes from `main`.
Easy.q: Which of the following statements accurately describe `git rebase`? (Select all that apply)
options: It rewrites the commit history of your feature branch.
It places your feature commits directly on top of the latest main commits.
It creates a dedicated 'Merge pull request' commit.
It prevents the creation of a linear project history.
It changes the cryptographic hashes (SHAs) of your existing commits.
a: It rewrites the commit history of your feature branch.
It places your feature commits directly on top of the latest main commits.
It changes the cryptographic hashes (SHAs) of your existing commits.
Easy.explanation: Rebasing lifts your local commits and replays them on top of the new base branch. Because the parent commit changes, the cryptographic hash of every commit changes, rewriting history. It *creates* a linear history by avoiding merge commits.

Easy.scenario: You have successfully rebased your local branch. You try to push it to your remote repository, but Git rejects it, stating: `Updates were rejected because the tip of your current branch is behind its remote counterpart.`
Easy.q: What command must you use to successfully push your rebased branch?
options: git push --force-with-lease
git pull origin branch-name
git merge main
git push --rebase
Easy.a: git push --force-with-lease
Easy.explanation: Because a rebase rewrites local commit history, your local branch no longer matches the remote branch history. A standard `git push` fails. You must force the push. `--force-with-lease` is safer than `--force` because it verifies nobody else has pushed commits to the remote branch in the meantime.

Easy.q: During a code review, an architect rejects this code because of a flaky behavior pattern. Why?
options: Hardcoded timeouts (waitForTimeout) create race conditions; if the app takes 5.1 seconds to load, the test fails, and if it takes 1 second, you waste 4 seconds.
The '#login' locator is invalid syntax.
Playwright does not support the 'waitForTimeout' method.
The test lacks a try/catch block.
Easy.a: Hardcoded timeouts (waitForTimeout) create race conditions; if the app takes 5.1 seconds to load, the test fails, and if it takes 1 second, you waste 4 seconds.
Easy.explanation: Hardcoded sleeps (`waitForTimeout`) are the #1 cause of flaky tests in UI automation. They never adapt to dynamic network speeds. Tests should use auto-waiting locators or `expect(locator).toBeVisible()` to dynamically proceed as soon as the element is ready.

Medium.scenario: You are deep in the middle of a complex rebase. You realize you have messed up the conflict resolutions and the files are completely broken.
Medium.q: What command instantly aborts the rebase and returns your repository to the exact state it was in before you started?
options: git rebase --abort
git reset --hard HEAD
git checkout -- .
git clean -fd
Medium.a: git rebase --abort
Medium.explanation: Git tracks the state of the branch before the rebase started. Running `git rebase --abort` safely cancels the operation, removes all temporary rebase files, and restores your branch to its original state.

Medium.code:
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in package.json
